evidence.clarity: 390: the headline says what the council will decide on your street, and the lede explains the plain-language digest and neighbourhood alert. The form makes the next step explicit.
evidence.fit: The page addresses residents and the English-only summary limit, but gives city clerks/funders no separate material and does not offer the Spanish alert email that a Spanish-speaking resident could use.
evidence.distinctiveness: The yellow-highlighted agenda entries and source links make the digest specific to council items; the visual language is neutral and does not suggest support for either side of a vote.
evidence.proof: At 1440 the labeled sample agenda is visible beside signup; selecting Riverbend changes the alert to item 8.A, and its “Open item” link leads to the supplied sample agenda-item page.
evidence.craft: At 390 the two-column desktop hero becomes a clear single column with a compact Menu button; the labels and 48px controls remain legible and the form stays within the viewport.
evidence.mobile: 390: the Menu button opens the page links and closes when pressed again; the alert artifact is below the first screen, but the neighborhood, email, CTA and English-only notice are visible before scrolling.
evidence.honesty: The sample says it is illustrative and “Not a record of any real council.” A valid submit then says “Not sent yet” and that the address was not stored, but this fact comes after pressing the button.
evidence.interaction: At 390, empty submission says “Choose a neighbourhood first”; after selecting Riverbend and entering an address it explicitly says nothing was sent, and changing to Old Town highlights item 9.C. At 1440/768 the five options also update matches.
evidence.copy: “A model drafts each summary, a volunteer checks it” and “every one links to the original item” answer what the service does without promising a political conclusion; “Always free” and the one-email frequency are clear.
evidence.first_screen: 1440: the CTA and labelled example digest share the first view. At 390 the CTA is visible but the sample artifact is not, so a phone visitor cannot yet judge the kind of alert.

problems: Sign-up only displays that nothing was sent and the address was not stored, leaving the resident with no path to actually join the list.
No separate clerk/funder section explains the pilot, its lack of partners or how a city could work with it.
A Spanish-speaking resident can read the English-only caveat, but cannot request an alert email in Spanish.

evidence.clarity: 1440: the lede says the city agenda is converted from a long PDF into plain-language items and emailed by neighbourhood/topic; the form asks for the neighbourhood and email.
evidence.fit: The Spanish checkbox requests Spanish alert mail and says summaries remain English; “For clerks and funders” separately states no partner cities, no funding and no reader counts, which is useful to both buyer audiences.
evidence.distinctiveness: The alert card resembles an actual email and the agenda/summary pairing explains the product’s job, with the highlighted street carried through the example.
evidence.proof: 1440: selecting Mill District changes the alert subject and highlighted location, and “Open the original agenda item” loads the local agenda page. However the later section calls this a real item although its details are absent from the brief.
evidence.craft: 1440: the serif display text, pale-blue card and yellow match highlight create a credible civic-publication feel; the probe reports one serious contrast violation and the mobile header becomes several lines.
evidence.mobile: 390: all navigation links stay expanded above the hero, and the primary action and alert card fall below the first viewport. At 320 the same stacked header takes substantial space.
evidence.honesty: The “How it works” section calls the October 28 item real and identifies Linden Falls and volunteer checkers even though none of those facts appears in the client brief; this undermines the trust expected of a neutral public-interest service.
evidence.interaction: At 390, “Get alerts for your street” scrolls to the form; choosing Eastgate changes the alert to “Nothing about Eastgate,” the Spanish checkbox toggles, and a valid address reveals a manual email handoff. All seven areas update at 1440 and 768 too.
evidence.copy: The form’s Spanish microcopy separates alert language from summary language; clerk/funder copy directly says “None yet” for partners and funding and explains what a city would be asked to do.
evidence.first_screen: 1440: the decision-specific promise, alert card and form are together. At 390 the headline is visible, but the stacked navigation and lede keep the action and proof outside the first screen.

problems: The page calls the October 28 agenda item real and names a city and volunteer checkers that the brief never supplies.
At 390 the expanded navigation pushes signup and the alert sample out of the opening viewport.
The form only explains the hand-written email handoff after submission, so the resident cannot see that commitment before tapping.

hard_fail_flags.evidence: B says “Here is one real item from the October 28 agenda,” identifies Linden Falls and named volunteer checkers, and includes specific agenda content that the brief does not supply.
hard_fail_flags.steps: Open B/index.html and follow “How it works” to the agenda/summary comparison. Read the sentence above the pair and the city/volunteer attribution; compare those claimed facts with the client brief, which names no city, agenda item or volunteers.

reason: A is the safer page to place under the founder’s name because it labels its agenda as illustrative and does not pass invented pilot material off as a real city record. B offers the more useful Spanish-alert option, a manual signup route and a strong clerk/funder path, but the false provenance is a serious trust break; I would reconsider if the example facts were substantiated and the mobile signup moved into view.
